messages.author: 7dfb45b1bf1d7262
messages.subject: Multigroup CFA Fit index improves with more constraints
parts:
Hi, I would love to get some help.

We are developing a new 10-item scale (4-point Likert response), 
after splitting my sample into 2 groups, one for EFA and one for CFA - it was found that a 2-factor oblique model best suits our data.

I then want to conduct a multigroup CFA , this time using the full sample but split into 4 subgroups (younger/older; males/females), hoping to be able to say that our scale, with such 2-factor oblique model, has measurement invariance across different age and gender groups.

To make such a claim, literature seems to suggest that the 3 invariance below needs to be confirmed:
Configural invariance (baseline)
Threshold invariance (group.equal = c("thresholds"))
Metric invariance (group.equal = c("thresholds","loadings"))

I have used the code below to examine these 3 invariances:

model_base <- '
personal =~ OBP10 + OBP02 + BP05 + BP04 + OBP09 + BP13; 
relational =~ OBR14 + OBR03 + OBR15 + OBR18
'
riskweb_df_e<-riskweb_df %>% select(OBP10,OBP02,BP05,BP04,OBP09,BP13,OBR14,OBR03,OBR15,OBR18,multigroup)

vars<-c("OBP10", "OBP02", "OBR03", "BP04", "BP05", "OBP09", "BP13", "OBR14", "OBR15", "OBR18")

baseline <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = model_base, data = riskweb_df_e, ordered = vars, ID.fac = "std.lv", ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016",group = "multigroup")

threshold <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = model_base, data = riskweb_df_e, ordered = vars, ID.fac = "std.lv", ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016", group = "multigroup",
                          group.equal = c("thresholds"))

loadings <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = gnrq_e_model_base,data = riskweb_df_e,ordered = vars, ID.fac = "std.lv", ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016", group = "multigroup", group.equal = c("thresholds","loadings"))

model.baseline <- as.character(baseline)
model.threshold <- as.character(threshold)
model.loadings <- as.character(loadings)

fit.baseline <- cfa(model.baseline, data = riskweb_df_e, group = "multigroup",
                    ordered = vars)
fit.threshold <- cfa(model.threshold, data = riskweb_df_e, group = "multigroup",
                     ordered = vars)
fit.loadings <- cfa(model.loadings, data = riskweb_df_e, group = "multigroup",
                    ordered = vars)

I got the following output:


The fit index improved with more constraints so I suspected that maybe my models were not nested, upon checking with the code below:

semTools::net(fit.baseline, fit.threshold)

I got:
Error in lav_partable_flat(FLAT, blocks = "group", meanstructure = meanstructure,  : 
  lavaan ERROR: expected 0 threshold(s) for variable ‘OBP10’; syntax contains 3

Error in lavInspect(newFit, "converged") : object 'newFit' not found

I have also tried using theta by adding the following line into the measEq.syntax()
parameterization = "theta"

and receiving warnings for "threshold" and "loading" models respectively below (not for baseline)
Warning message:
In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
  lavaan WARNING:
    The variance-covariance matrix of the estimated parameters (vcov)
    does not appear to be positive definite! The smallest eigenvalue
    (= 4.045876e-17) is close to zero. This may be a symptom that the
    model is not identified.
Warning message:
In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
  lavaan WARNING:
    The variance-covariance matrix of the estimated parameters (vcov)
    does not appear to be positive definite! The smallest eigenvalue
    (= 7.705828e-17) is close to zero. This may be a symptom that the
    model is not identified.

(theta) Result:


My data is highly skewed - I am wondering if that could be a reason but have limited knowledge in CFA so would much appreciate any help on this.

Thanks and Best Wishes,
Crystal

messages.author: 12fdd832cacb825e
messages.subject: Re: Multigroup CFA Fit index improves with more constraints
parts:
Crystal,

First, with ordered data, threshold and loading invariance should be tested simultaneously, not separately.

Second, the chi-square and df are increasing as you constrain the model, as would be expected (though isn't necessarily going to happen with scaled fit stats). Other fit indices do not necessarily follow this, as most take parsimony into account in some way.

Looking at chi-squared, even the configural model doesn't fit well. Looking at measures of approximate fit, all the models fit reasonably well by common criteria. So you need to decide what you want to focus on for your fit assessment.

As far as the warnings (which are not errors and not necessarily fatal to interpretation), how large are your subgroups in the CFA sample? You've cut this a lot of ways. You might be running into empirical under-identification.

Pat

messages.subject: Re: Multigroup CFA Fit index improves with more constraints
parts:
Crystal,

Interleaved:

First, with ordered data, threshold and loading invariance should be tested simultaneously, not separately.
> I would then only compare 2 models (Configural and "threshold and loading")
Correct.

Looking at chi-squared, even the configural model doesn't fit well. Looking at measures of approximate fit, all the models fit reasonably well by common criteria. So you need to decide what you want to focus on for your fit assessment.
> This may be due to the large sample size I have (total n=2984 before splitting into subgroups) -> I wonder if other model fits are reasonably well, would I be able to say that my construct has good measure invariance across gender and age.

This is subject to debate. Depending on your field, finding approximate fit indices above common criteria in the most constrained model may be sufficient. But you might also do well to look at residuals and score tests to localize the poor absolute fit (one large residual is probably more of a danger sign than a group of small ones that have the same impact on fit measures.)

As far as the warnings (which are not errors and not necessarily fatal to interpretation), how large are your subgroups in the CFA sample? You've cut this a lot of ways. You might be running into empirical under-identification.
> The sample sizes and results are as below:
Those sample sizes should be fine. I wouldn't worry too much about the warning.

Another concern of mine is that when using the code below to calculate the change of chisq between the 2 models, the result was a significant change (not invariance).

lavTestLRT(fit.baseline,fit.loadings)
Scaled Chi-Squared Difference Test (method = “satorra.2000”)
lavaan NOTE:
    The “Chisq” column contains standard test statistics, not the
    robust test that should be reported per model. A robust difference
    test is a function of two standard (not robust) statistics.
 
              Df AIC BIC  Chisq Chisq diff Df diff Pr(>Chisq)    
fit.baseline 136         331.84                                  
fit.loadings 190         616.18     137.88      54  2.847e-09 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

Two things: This is subject to the same concerns about chi-squared detecting small differences as the full model fit test is. Second, strictly speaking, it only holds if the full model fits by chi-square. I would focus more on residuals in the constrained model than this test.

Pat

Again, very much appreciated your help on this!
Best Wishes,
Crystal

Hi Patrick,

Thank you very much for all the useful advice, I have never looked into the residuals part and would study more on its implications in CFA-MG.

But you might also do well to look at residuals and score tests to localize the poor absolute fit (one large residual is probably more of a danger sign than a group of small ones that have the same impact on fit measures.)

> I have looked into them using the code below, but am not sure the "cut-off" value to be considered as a large residual (would look into more literature):
lavResiduals(fit.loadings)
checking the output of $cov for each of the four sub-groups by looking at (one example below):
$`older females`$cov

Many thanks and Best Wishes,
Crystal

On Monday, 21 December 2020 at 03:42:42 UTC+9 mal...@malonequantitative.com wrote:
Crystal,

Interleaved:

First, with ordered data, threshold and loading invariance should be tested simultaneously, not separately.
> I would then only compare 2 models (Configural and "threshold and loading")


Correct.
 
Looking at chi-squared, even the configural model doesn't fit well. Looking at measures of approximate fit, all the models fit reasonably well by common criteria. So you need to decide what you want to focus on for your fit assessment.
> This may be due to the large sample size I have (total n=2984 before splitting into subgroups) -> I wonder if other model fits are reasonably well, would I be able to say that my construct has good measure invariance across gender and age.


This is subject to debate. Depending on your field, finding approximate fit indices above common criteria in the most constrained model may be sufficient. But you might also do well to look at residuals and score tests to localize the poor absolute fit (one large residual is probably more of a danger sign than a group of small ones that have the same impact on fit measures.)
 
As far as the warnings (which are not errors and not necessarily fatal to interpretation), how large are your subgroups in the CFA sample? You've cut this a lot of ways. You might be running into empirical under-identification.
> The sample sizes and results are as below:



Those sample sizes should be fine. I wouldn't worry too much about the warning.
 
Another concern of mine is that when using the code below to calculate the change of chisq between the 2 models, the result was a significant change (not invariance).

lavTestLRT(fit.baseline,fit.loadings)
Scaled Chi-Squared Difference Test (method = “satorra.2000”)
lavaan NOTE:
    The “Chisq” column contains standard test statistics, not the
    robust test that should be reported per model. A robust difference
    test is a function of two standard (not robust) statistics.
 
              Df AIC BIC  Chisq Chisq diff Df diff Pr(>Chisq)    
fit.baseline 136         331.84                                  
fit.loadings 190         616.18     137.88      54  2.847e-09 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1



Two things: This is subject to the same concerns about chi-squared detecting small differences as the full model fit test is. Second, strictly speaking, it only holds if the full model fits by chi-square. I would focus more on residuals in the constrained model than this test.

Pat
 
Again, very much appreciated your help on this!
Best Wishes,
Crystal





On Mon, 21 Dec 2020 at 02:36, Patrick (Malone Quantitative) <mal...@malonequantitative.com> wrote:
Crystal,

First, with ordered data, threshold and loading invariance should be tested simultaneously, not separately.

Second, the chi-square and df are increasing as you constrain the model, as would be expected (though isn't necessarily going to happen with scaled fit stats). Other fit indices do not necessarily follow this, as most take parsimony into account in some way.

Looking at chi-squared, even the configural model doesn't fit well. Looking at measures of approximate fit, all the models fit reasonably well by common criteria. So you need to decide what you want to focus on for your fit assessment.

As far as the warnings (which are not errors and not necessarily fatal to interpretation), how large are your subgroups in the CFA sample? You've cut this a lot of ways. You might be running into empirical under-identification.

Pat

As far as the warnings (which are not errors and not necessarily fatal to interpretation), how large are your subgroups in the CFA sample? You've cut this a lot of ways. You might be running into empirical under-identification.
> The sample sizes and results are as below:



Those sample sizes should be fine. I wouldn't worry too much about the warning.
 
Another concern of mine is that when using the code below to calculate the change of chisq between the 2 models, the result was a significant change (not invariance).

Two things: This is subject to the same concerns about chi-squared detecting small differences as the full model fit test is. Second, strictly speaking, it only holds if the full model fits by chi-square. I would focus more on residuals in the constrained model than this test.

On Mon, 21 Dec 2020 at 02:36, Patrick (Malone Quantitative) <mal...@malonequantitative.com> wrote:
Crystal,

First, with ordered data, threshold and loading invariance should be tested simultaneously, not separately.

Second, the chi-square and df are increasing as you constrain the model, as would be expected (though isn't necessarily going to happen with scaled fit stats). Other fit indices do not necessarily follow this, as most take parsimony into account in some way.

Looking at chi-squared, even the configural model doesn't fit well. Looking at measures of approximate fit, all the models fit reasonably well by common criteria. So you need to decide what you want to focus on for your fit assessment.

As far as the warnings (which are not errors and not necessarily fatal to interpretation), how large are your subgroups in the CFA sample? You've cut this a lot of ways. You might be running into empirical under-identification.

Pat
